key_insight: A controlled, multi-model human study shows that providing novices with LLM assistance often improves performance on biosecurity-relevant in silico biology tasks compared with internet-only access, though the size of uplift varies by task and model—highlighting both scientific acceleration and dual‑use risk tradeoffs.
problem_solved: Quantifies whether and how much LLMs enable novice users to do better on computational biology tasks than they would using standard internet resources, addressing uncertainty about human uplift and downstream dual-use implications.
method: Multi-model, multi-benchmark human uplift experiment: novices randomized to LLM access vs internet-only across eight biosecurity-relevant task sets.
Measured task performance (objective scores) and behavior (queries, reliance on model), with comparison across models, benchmarks, and task types.
Combined quantitative performance metrics with qualitative analysis to characterize where LLMs help, fail, or introduce risk.
impact: Provides empirical evidence for AI/ML practitioners and policy makers about how LLMs change human capability on sensitive biology tasks, informing risk assessment, model deployment choices, and mitigation strategies for dual-use scenarios.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing average novice performance: LLM-assisted vs internet-only across the eight task sets.
Flow diagram of experimental design: participant recruitment → randomization → task blocks → outcome measurement.
Heatmap showing uplift magnitude by (model × task) to highlight where assistance is most/least effective.
Risk–benefit scale icon or quadrant summarizing tasks with high uplift and high dual‑use concern vs low uplift/low concern.
paper_title: LLM Novice Uplift on Dual-Use, In Silico Biology Tasks
paper_authors: Chen Bo Calvin Zhang, Christina Q. Knight, Nicholas Kruus, Jason Hausenloy, Pedro Medeiros
